title: Investigating the Relationship between Noise Exposure and Human Cognitive Performance: Attention, Stress, and Mental Workload Based on EEG Signals Using Power Spectrum Density
research_question: To investigate the relationship between noise exposure (type and level) and human cognitive abilities (attention, stress, mental workload, and behavioral performance) using power spectrum density (PSD) derived from EEG signals and the Stroop Color-Word Test (SCWT).

participants.description: 24 students (12 males, 12 females) from Indonesia. Divided into two groups (12 participants each, 6 males/6 females) for continuous vs. intermittent noise exposure. Participants had no color blindness, no prior cardiovascular disorders, refrained from alcohol/caffeine for 12h, maintained a normal BMI (18.5-25.0 kg/m²), had no history of sleep disturbances, and scored normally on the DASS-21 questionnaire.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Industrial machinery noise at 6 levels: 55 dB, 65 dB, 70 dB, 75 dB, 80 dB, and 85 dB. Two types: continuous and intermittent. Intermittent noise involved 20s high-level, switch to low-level, 5s no noise, then repeat 20s. Continuous noise was constant fixed noise. Sound was modified using Adobe Premiere Pro and played via audio speakers on a smart TV.

measures.instrument: Stroop Color-Word Test (SCWT) total response time
EEG Beta band power spectrum density (AF3, AF4, F3, F4 channels, 12.5–30 Hz)
EEG Alpha band power spectrum density (F7, F8 channels, 8–12.5 Hz)
EEG Theta-to-alpha ratio (AF3, AF4, F3, F4, F7, F8, FC5, FC6 channels)

findings.consequent: Males' total response time on SCWT
findings.mechanism: Males tend to experience greater noise impact on response time scores.
findings.quote: The average total response time of continuous noise for males exceeded that of females in groups exposed to noise levels of 55 dB, 65 dB, 70 dB, 75 dB, 80 dB, and 85 dB.

findings.consequent: Males' total response time on SCWT
findings.mechanism: Males tend to experience greater noise impact on response time scores.
findings.quote: Likewise, for intermittent noise, the average total response time for males surpassed that of females in groups affected by noise levels higher than 55 dB, 65 dB, 70 dB, 75 dB, 80 dB, and 85 dB.

findings.mechanism: Males are more likely to be affected by continuous noise exposure than females in terms of accuracy.
findings.quote: The average accuracy score in the continuous noise category for the female group was lower than the average score for males in the group exposed to higher noise levels at 55 dB, 65 dB, 70 dB, 75 dB, 80 dB, and 85 dB.

findings.mechanism: Females are more likely to experience high intermittent noise exposure than males in terms of accuracy.
findings.quote: For intermittent noise, males' average accuracy scores fell below the average for females in the group who experienced higher noise levels at 55 dB, 65 dB, 70 dB, 75 dB, 80 dB, and 85 dB.

findings.antecedent: Noise type (continuous/intermittent) and noise level (55-85 dB)
findings.consequent: SCWT total response time and accuracy
findings.mechanism: Noise content and levels significantly affect cognitive performance.
findings.quote: The Kruskal-Wallis ANOVA results on response time and accuracy with continuous and intermittent types of noise showed that the effect of the content and noise levels was statistically significant across the response time and accuracy (Chi-square = 11.07, df = 5, p < 0.05)

findings.consequent: Attention (EEG Beta log power spectrum density)
findings.mechanism: Highest beta power spectrum log value and lowest frequency value (13.2 Hz) indicate best attentional conditions.
findings.quote: Participants showed that they had the best attentional conditions at a noise level of 65 dB based on the highest power spectrum log value compared to other noise levels.

findings.consequent: Attention (EEG Beta log power spectrum density)
findings.mechanism: Highest beta power spectrum log value and lowest frequency value (12.7 Hz) indicate best attentional conditions.
findings.quote: Based on the average log power spectrum, the noise level of 65 dB gives the largest average log power spectrum with the value of 35.01 µV2, and the maximum point is at a log power of 37.36 µV2 at a frequency of 12.7 Hz.

findings.consequent: Attention interference (EEG Beta log power spectrum density)
findings.mechanism: Higher noise levels lead to greater attention interference.
findings.quote: Based on the results of this experiment, continuous noise at a noise level of 80 dB has the highest influence on attention interference

findings.consequent: Attention interference (EEG Beta log power spectrum density)
findings.mechanism: Higher noise levels lead to greater attention interference.
findings.quote: while intermittent noise at a noise level of 85 dB has the highest influence on participants.

findings.consequent: Relaxed state (EEG Alpha log power spectrum density)
findings.mechanism: Largest alpha power spectrum log value (41.31 µV² at 8.13 Hz) indicates a relaxed condition (not experiencing stress).
findings.quote: participants were in a relaxed condition (not experiencing stress) at a noise level of 65 dB at exposure to the type of continuous noise based on the largest power spectrum at the level of 65 dB, with the maximum point being at a log power of 41.31 µV2 at a frequency of 8.13 Hz.

findings.consequent: Relaxed state (EEG Alpha log power spectrum density)
findings.mechanism: Largest alpha power spectrum log value (39.44 µV² at 8.13 Hz) indicates a relaxed condition (not experiencing stress).
findings.quote: For the type of intermittent noise, participants at the 65 dB noise level are in a relaxed condition with the largest power spectrum at the 65 dB level, with the maximum point being at a log power of 39.44 µV2 at a frequency of 8.13 Hz.

findings.consequent: Stress (EEG Alpha log power spectrum density)
findings.mechanism: Lowest alpha signal power spectrum value indicates a state of stress.
findings.quote: A noise level of 80 dB in the continuous noise type [...] has the lowest alpha signal power spectrum value, so participants are in a state of stress at those noise levels.

findings.consequent: Stress (EEG Alpha log power spectrum density)
findings.mechanism: Lowest alpha signal power spectrum value indicates a state of stress.
findings.quote: A noise level of [...] 75 dB in the intermittent noise type has the lowest alpha signal power spectrum value, so participants are in a state of stress at those noise levels.

findings.antecedent: Noise level (70 dB and above) (continuous and intermittent)
findings.mechanism: Increased theta-to-alpha ratio indicates the presence of mental workload.
findings.quote: at a noise level of 70 dB with a theta-to-alpha ratio value that increased from the noise level below, participants started mentioning how noise affected their mental workload.

findings.consequent: Mental workload index value (EEG Theta-to-alpha ratio)
findings.mechanism: The relationship between noise level and mental workload is linear; greater noise leads to greater mental workload.
findings.quote: Figure 8 shows that the increase in mental workload index value in continuous and intermittent noise is linear to the noise level. The greater the noise, the greater the mental workload index value.

findings.consequent: Mental workload index value (EEG Theta-to-alpha ratio)
findings.mechanism: Continuous noise leads to higher mental workload compared to intermittent noise.
findings.quote: Based on Figure 8, the continuous noise mental workload index value is greater than the intermittent noise mental workload index.

findings.antecedent: High power spectrum density values at frontal lobe electrodes (AF3, AF4, F3, F4, F7, F8)
findings.mechanism: High PSD values in frontal regions are associated with attentional processing, stress, and mental workload.
findings.quote: The topography at electrodes AF3, AF4, F3, F4, F7, and F8 marked in red at the frontal lobe position shows high power spectrum density values indicating the strong activation of frontal brain areas associated with attentional processing, stress, and mental workload.

mechanisms: Noise can promote arousal and provide excitement for uninteresting tasks, boosting attention and task participation.
Noise can decrease accuracy but speed up reaction times due to an accuracy-speed tradeoff.
Higher log power spectrum density values and lower frequency values in beta bands indicate higher attention and concentration.
Lower log power spectrum density values in beta bands indicate attention interference.
Increased alpha band power spectrum indicates decreased brain activity and a relaxed state.
Decreased alpha band power spectrum indicates a state of stress.
An increase in theta strength and a decrease in alpha strength in the frontal brain region are associated with an increase in mental workload.
Increased noise levels lead to increased mental workload.
moderators: Noise level (55 dB, 65 dB, 70 dB, 75 dB, 80 dB, 85 dB)
implementation_implications: Develop environmental policies regulating noise levels in workplaces, schools, and urban areas to protect health and cognitive performance.
Implement stricter standards for noise levels.
Schedule cognitive tasks to avoid high levels of environmental noise.
Perform jobs requiring high concentration when environmental noise is minimal.

tables.description: Relationship between total response time on continuous and intermittent noise levels.
Relationship between accuracy on continuous and intermittent noise levels.
Log power spectrum of attention within continuous noise (a) and intermittent noise (b).

Relationship between the mental workload index and continuous and intermittent noise levels.
Topographic mapping of the relative power of frequency bands during continuous noise exposure (a) and intermittent noise exposure (b).

limitations: Data collection was conducted in a laboratory setting, limiting ecological validity.
Variable noise sources were observed from only one sound source (industrial machinery).
The exposure period to noise was shorter than would typically occur in real work environments, potentially leading to smaller observed impacts.
The sole metric used to assess cognitive aptitude was the power spectrum density of the EEG.

crossref_abstract: A pervasive environmental stressor is one that damages mental and physical health as well as cognitive abilities by producing noise at a specific frequency and level. Current noise pollution levels pose a significant threat to public health, potentially leading to impaired cognitive function, increased stress, and other negative health consequences. This study aims to investigate the relationship between noise exposure and human cognitive abilities using a comprehensive analysis of power spectrum density (PSD) derived from EEG signals. Twenty-four participants completed the experiment to identify the effect of exposure to different noise levels (55 dB, 65 dB, 70 dB, 75 dB, 80 dB, and 85 dB) and two types of continuous and intermittent noise. The Stroop Color–Word Test and the Emotive Epoch EEG are cognitive task instruments used during experiments. Behavioral performance (accuracy and response time) and power spectrum electroencephalographic density were collected and analyzed. The methodology involved collecting EEG data from participants exposed to controlled noise stimuli and a subsequent PSD analysis to uncover frequency-specific patterns associated with cognitive processes. Attention levels were measured by examining beta wave activity, while stress responses were evaluated through an alpha wave analysis. Additionally, mental workload was assessed by considering the overall distribution of PSD through the theta-to-alpha ratio. The results revealed a significant relationship between the exposure to noise types and levels and human cognitive ability. The analysis of the power spectrum density on the cognitive aspects of attention and stress yielded results indicating that participants were in the best attention condition and in a relaxed or unstressed state when exposed to noise levels of 65 dB in both continuous and intermittent noise types. For the mental workload aspect, participants exposed to both continuous and intermittent noise types at a noise level of 70 dB began to indicate the presence of mental workload. These findings supported the importance of considering the impact of environmental noise on human cognitive well-being and demonstrated the potential of EEG monitoring as an objective tool for assessing the impact of noise on cognitive performance.
